toc.title: Fight is meant to be one big burst
How we get stuck in fight
Frozen fight and everyday fight feel different
Your stuck state has an impulse

blocks.p: What are the best ways to come out of a polyvagal fight state? Should you scream into a pillow? Should you punch things? Can it help to use your imagination? Is there one right way to climb the polyvagal ladder out of fight?
One listener asked:

q: I was just wondering if you've done an episode yet on the best ways to get out of the fight state, to move up the polyvagal ladder. ... Is screaming into or punching a pillow ever a good idea?

blocks.p: Let's do a quick review. The Polyvagal Theory is an explanation for how mammals connect, but also for how we make adjustments in order to survive a threat in the moment. We go through autonomic responses. They're not thought out, they're not planned, they're not a conscious thing. They're hardwired. They're in our DNA. These autonomic responses improve the chances of survival and optimize resources. If the body's prepared for safety, it optimizes the resources within it. Same thing for running away, fighting, or immobilizing.
One of those autonomic responses is preparation for fight, or for aggression. Here's how we get there, down the polyvagal ladder:

ol: When there's a potential danger and we can't use our capacity for connection, our safety state, we drop down the polyvagal ladder into the flight state.
If we can't run away, if we can't escape the situation, we drop down even further into the fight state.

blocks.p: Flight and fight are both a sympathetic state, but they have distinct behaviors associated with them, and when we get stuck in them, they have distinct feelings and thoughts. So I separate them. Flight is the first behavioral attempt, and then we drop further into fight. If we can't escape and run away, we become more aggressive in order to get the danger to back off, so that we can escape.

blocks.h: Fight is meant to be one big burst

blocks.p: Flight and fight are supposed to be used quickly, in one large burst of sympathetic activity. They're not supposed to stay in our system for a long time.

Fight is there to aggress upon a danger, to repel it. It's supposed to be one large burst of movement: pushing, shoving, hitting, throwing, lifting. Once fight creates space and the danger backs off, we use flight to create more space and actually get away. Then we get back to our family or our herd or our tribe, back to safety, and we reconnect with safe others and with ourselves.

That's what it evolved within us to do. But as human beings, we have this knack for getting stuck in defensive states, and that's called trauma: being stuck in a defensive state. People can get stuck down the polyvagal ladder on the fight rung.

blocks.h: How we get stuck in fight

blocks.p: This can look a few different ways.

ol: Chronic disruption of connectedness. Maybe developmentally there was a constant severing of connection with caregivers, trusted adults, the people we were supposed to rely on. Through that constant severing, maybe we had to exist in a fight state in order to get our needs met. So we just kind of exist more in a fight state.

An acute life threat reaction. We went through an incident where we had to go into a fight state, but we weren't able to use that fight energy, and it got stuck in the system. We were in fight but immobilized, either through force or because we perceived that fight wouldn't be able to deal with the situation. That's the freeze mixed state of the Polyvagal Theory: flight and fight active plus shutdown, sympathetic plus dorsal vagal. We're ready to run or fight, but also immobilized, and the flight and fight energy is frozen into the system.

Coming out of shutdown up into fight. Shutdown is the bottom of the ladder: immobilization, limp collapse. As we come up out of it into fight, the sympathetic fight energy comes back into the system. It wasn't stuck there; we just weren't accessing it. I don't think that's what this listener is asking about, but it could be a factor for somebody.

blocks.h: Frozen fight and everyday fight feel different

blocks.p: Within freeze, we could have a more fight-flavored freeze, which I'd associate more with rage, or a more flight-flavored freeze, which I'd associate more with panic.

Chronic disruption of connectedness will definitely leave someone down their polyvagal ladder, but not necessarily with the immobilization along with it. Someone who lived in that chronic disruption might just get stuck in flight energy. Day to day, they have a noticeable amount of anxiety, which is the day-to-day experience of a stuck flight state. That's different from being stuck in a flight-flavored freeze and having panic attacks. Freeze and panic attacks really go hand in hand.

Same thing with the person stuck in fight. They may have gotten their needs met by existing in a fight state, so they kind of live there, but without the immobilization. They might feel angry or irritable underneath it all. That fight energy affects them: they think more in terms of blame, or think more negatively, and they feel more irritation and anger and snap at people. It's in the system, but with no immobilization, there's no explosive rage coming from a frozen fight state.

blocks.h: Your stuck state has an impulse

blocks.p: Our polyvagal states have impulses, all of them. The impulse from the safety state is to connect. The impulse from the flight state is to escape, to run, to mobilize and get to safety.

In very, very simple terms, being stuck down the ladder indicates that there might be an impulse that hasn't been acted on yet, an impulse within you that hasn't been able to complete. If you had an impulse to shove or hit or throw, but you were immobilized during that impulse, the immobility could freeze that sympathetic activation in your body and leave you in a frozen fight state.
So what's the best way to release a stuck fight state? It's different for all of us. You need to be curious about what impulse is stemming from your stuck polyvagal state.

I've worked with clients who have a scream that wants to come out. I've worked with clients who have squeezing they need to act on. For me, I've existed more in shutdown, and as I come more and more out of it, there's some fight energy I'm still learning how to feel and welcome. I notice that pulling feels fantastic when I have more fight in my system. When I'm in a little more of a dysregulated fight state, I go to these spiky rubber rings, hedgehog rings I think they're called, and I pull on them. Something feels like it releases, and it really eases my body up.
So maybe there's a physical impulse you can act on that feels relieving. Maybe it's screaming. Maybe it's hitting a pillow. Sure.

But fight can also be released without physically acting on the impulse. For myself and for clients, simply using the imagination mindfully can allow a discharge to happen. Peter Levine has talked about this as well. Mindfully using your imagination, mindfully attuning to what's happening within you, just through your awareness, can help release whatever is stuck inside of you, even if you're not actually getting up and running away. You can mindfully tune in to the stuck energy as it is and allow a discharge to happen, if you can handle that.

Think about Peter Levine's example of Nancy and the tiger. That was his first therapy client, where she went into the shaking and trembling trauma release. She was already kind of in that state, with the immobility in her system, and he gave her an imaginary image of being chased by a tiger. That allowed her to enter into the shaking and trembling, which released at least some of the stuck sympathetic state inside her.

I've seen this with my own clients. I had a teen client imagining running home to her grandmother's house, which was her safe place. She mindfully got into the imaginative experience of running there, and that caused her to go into shaking and trembling and release some of what she was going through.

I had an adult male client who was able to mindfully experience his body's sensations. It was more of the fight flavor. He simply attuned to it mindfully and really felt it without judgment, and his breath spontaneously began to heave: big gasps of air in, then letting it out. He came out the other end of that and said, "Wow, I feel way different. I feel like something's been released." He was able to make more eye contact with me, connect, and feel pride in himself. He'd really relieved some of his stuck state.

I've also had many clients who go to the gym and use their fight state or their flight state there, mindfully using their muscles. So yes, you can definitely use your body, but you don't have to act directly on the impulse, like "I feel the impulse to scream," and let it out. You can do something extremely physical and challenging, like a workout, and allow yourself to feel some anger, or feel the sensations of your stuck fight state, to help release bits and pieces of it, titrating it. Clients have found that helpful. It builds their mindfulness of what they're going through and lets them have their feelings without judgment, let them be there, and then do something with them.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: What I want you to get from this: don't look for the right technique. Don't look for the right movement. There is no prescriptive "here's the thing you do."

I find it disturbing. I've seen videos of people saying, "Do this. Crane your neck this way. Arch your back that way. Rub this." No. That's not the way this works. That's nonsense. When it comes to you and your stuck state, your body knows far more than me, far more than any Instagram guru or 15-second TikTok video. I need you to believe that your body knows more than even your brain does, in a way. We need your brain, your consciousness, your awareness, your mindfulness, to be more attuned to what your body already knows. That's the goal. If you can do that, your body will tell you, "This feels right."
So instead, be curious. What do I want? What does my body want? What does my stuck state want? Be as curious as you can about what your body or your system needs.
Irene Lyon put it this way when she was on the podcast:

q: What can I do that will help my physiology come down? And that is trial and error and that's being experimental and curious.

blocks.p: I know this is difficult, because from a sympathetic state, from a stuck flight or fight state, we're more evaluative and less curious. We have more urgency and less patience. The mindfulness I'm talking about, aligning your brain to your body, really requires more patience and more curiosity.
Safety is the priority. Accessing your safety state is the priority. We're talking about fight here, but this works for any stuck defensive state.

ol: Ground in your safety state. Once you're grounded in safety, you can bring that to your stuck defensive state, whatever it is.
Allow the emotion. Maybe it's anger. Witness it and allow it to be there.
Drill down to the sensations underneath the emotion. Mindfully experience them.

Notice whether there's an impulse of what to do next. Maybe that's to continue with whatever images your brain is coming up with. Maybe it's to actively get up and do something with it. Maybe you do need to squeeze something.

blocks.p: If you can do that, more active ladder climbing will happen from there.
